doc.title: Vince DiMartino interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, January 8, 2025

title: Playing with Lionel Hampton at 19, and Wallace Davenport
summary: At about 19 he played in Hampton's big band and small group alongside Wallace Davenport, a circular-breathing trumpeter who studied French.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Playing in Lionel Hampton's big band

blocks.x: Yes. And when I played with Clark — with Lionel Hampton when I was, you know like 19, the band was Jimmy Cleveland, Julian Priester, Jerome Richardson came one time to be in Lionel Hampton’s big band at the Riverboat in the Empire State Building. And I was playing with Lionel Hampton. Paul Cohen, he was the lead trumpet in Count Basie at the time, so when he was in New York and they weren’t on tour he’d just play gigs around New York and I mean it was amazing. The whole thing was amazing, just that I could be in the band let alone — and then Lionel Hampton — oh I could tell you a million stories of Lionel Hampton, with Gladys, with his wife.
Yeah, we’ll do a part two. We should do it.

These stories with Lionel Hampton are unreal. Because I was like this little kid. You know I was scared of half the people in there because they were kind of rough. And I really wasn’t rough, you know. I was naïve and just trying to play good. And Wallace Davenport, did you know who he is?

Okay well Wallace was on the band, the small group. After I finished the big band job he asked me to play with this small group, and Wallace was the other trumpet. The guy was unreal. He could circular breathe on double high Cs. I go, “Wallace” and he was super nice. He studied French all the time on the bus. And I said, “Why are you studying — are you going to France?” He says, “No, no” he said, “I’m going back to New Orleans and a lot of the people that I hang out with, they speak French and I’m going to get much better at it.” And then he moved, maybe six, eight years later he moved back to New Orleans and stayed there the rest of his life and played in traditional jazz bands. You know I was lucky because I was the end of an era.
